fixes.explanation: This one is actually true, friend. Nehemiah says in verse 20, “Our God will fight for us!” That's how he finishes his instructions about the horn. The line is right there in the text.

Verse 1 says Sanballat was “…furious and filled with indignation.” Sanballat already mocked the rebuilding once (Nehemiah 2:19), and now he hears the wall is really going up and he does not take it well. I think his whole day just got ruined.

Not quite, friend. Sanballat asks, “Will they complete it in a day?” and I think he's poking fun at the builders, not complaining about their speed. He calls them “feeble” in verse 2. I think his other questions, like “Can they restore the wall by themselves?”, are about whether they can do it at all.

Yes, and Tobiah the Ammonite, who was beside Sanballat, is the one who says it. Right after Sanballat's questions, he says, “If even a fox were to climb up on what they are building, it would break down their wall of stones!” So the fox line is in the text, word for word.

That's his prayer in verse 4: “Turn their scorn back upon their own heads…” Nehemiah, who is leading the rebuilding, brings the mockery straight to God. He starts the prayer with “Hear us, O God, for we are despised.” He says it plainly.
That's the reason he gives. Verse 5 says, “…for they have provoked the builders.” The people working on the wall are the ones he names. Nehemiah brings that straight to God in his prayer.
The king isn't in this prayer at all. Verse 5 says, “…for they have provoked the builders.” That's the group Nehemiah names, the ones working on the wall.

Verse 6 says they rebuilt the wall “…until all of it was joined together up to half its height…” That means the whole wall is connected and halfway up. That's real progress after all that mockery. Halfway up is still a long way from done, and I think they know it.
They've done much more than that. Verse 6 says the whole wall was joined together “…up to half its height…” That's way past just getting started. Tobiah's fox would have a harder climb by now.
Verse 9 says, “So we prayed to our God…” Nehemiah tells it right in the same breath as the guard. Prayer is part of how they answer the threat, and it doesn't get skipped.
Nobody runs in verse 9. It says, “So we prayed to our God and posted a guard against them day and night.” The verse has them praying and posting a guard. Running isn't in the plan.
No letter gets sent in this verse. Verse 9 says they prayed and posted a guard against the enemies. Sending a letter isn't one of the things it lists.
A gate is a fine thing, but verse 9 doesn't post one. It says they “…posted a guard against them day and night.” A guard is what the verse names.
The text says otherwise. Verse 9 says they posted a guard “…day and night.” That means the watch runs after dark too, not just in daylight.

Two would be a polite heads-up, friend. Verse 12 says the Jews who lived nearby “…told us ten times over…” and their warning was, “Wherever you turn, they will attack us.” I think they really wanted to be heard.

Seven sounds like a solid guess, friend, but verse 12 says the Jews who lived nearby “…told us ten times over…” That's three more than seven. The warning they gave was, “Wherever you turn, they will attack us.”

Not quite, friend. Verse 13 says, “I stationed them by families with their swords, spears, and bows.” Nehemiah stations them by families, and nothing in the verse says he pulled the men away from their families. I think that's the opposite of sending each man off alone.

Right, nothing there separates the men from their families. Verse 13 says, “I stationed them by families with their swords, spears, and bows.” He stations them by families. I think that makes the posts mean a lot more.
That's his list in verse 14: “…fight for your brothers, your sons and your daughters, your wives and your homes.” He's naming the people and the homes. I think that's a lot to stand up for.
Verse 15 says, “…each of us returned to his own work on the wall.” Back to the wall they go. The scare doesn't send them home.

Marching out would make a great movie scene, but that's not what happens. Verse 15 says, “…each of us returned to his own work on the wall.” Their response is to get back to the work they were already doing.

Leaving Jerusalem would be a dramatic exit, friend, but the text has no one packing a bag. Verse 15 says, “…each of us returned to his own work on the wall.” Returned means back to the job, not out of the city.

That's the first half of the split. Verse 16 says, “…half of my servants did the work while the other half held spears, shields, bows, and armor.” Building and guarding both get covered, and I think that's a smart way to split a crew.
That's not what the horn is for. Nehemiah says, “Wherever you hear the sound of the horn, rally to us there.” The instruction is to rally to them, not to scatter to their homes.

Climbing isn't part of the instruction. Nehemiah says, “Wherever you hear the sound of the horn, rally to us there.” The instruction is to rally to where the horn sounds, and climbing isn't mentioned.
Verse 22 has Nehemiah say, “Let every man and his servant spend the night inside Jerusalem…” They stay in the city. Every man and his servant is included, so nobody is left out of the order.

Samaria shows up in verse 2, where Sanballat speaks before the army of Samaria. Nehemiah wants his people in Jerusalem. Verse 22 says, “Let every man and his servant spend the night inside Jerusalem…”
That's his reason in verse 22: “…so that they can stand guard by night and work by day.” So guard duty takes the night and the building takes the day. I think that's a full schedule for one crew.
Verse 23 ends, “each carried his weapon, even to go for water.” Even a simple trip for water comes with a weapon. I think that shows how alert they stay.
